claims.text: The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy is a single-phase BCC RHEA.
The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy has high density and poor room-temperature ductility.
Adding a minor concentration of Al to Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr will induce separation into ordered B2 and disordered BCC phases.
Controlled heat treatment can promote B2/BCC phase separation after Al addition.
The secondary B2 phase will have a reticulated-network morphology in the continuous BCC matrix.
The precipitated B2 phase will be a NiAl-type ordered intermetallic.
An inverted microstructure consisting of discrete B2 precipitates in a continuous BCC matrix can improve room-temperature compressive ductility while maintaining high yield strength.
The B2 network will deflect cracks and thereby mitigate catastrophic brittle fracture.
A continuous ordered B2 matrix causes poor room-temperature ductility in B2+BCC RHEAs.
The modified alloy will attain more than approximately 5-10% room-temperature compressive plastic strain and increased yield strength relative to the baseline.
Al addition will increase alloy density by less than 2%.
Al is a low-density alloying element relative to the high-density refractory constituents.
The desired property improvement requires an Al concentration low enough to avoid a continuous B2 matrix or excessive brittle intermetallic formation.
B2 formation in Al-modified Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr is thermodynamically plausible based on analogous Al-containing HEAs.
Annealing at 800-1000 °C is predicted to induce B2 precipitation in Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr-Al.
Al contents of 2, 5, and 8 at% span a useful range for testing the proposed transition between single-phase BCC, discrete B2 precipitation, and a continuous B2 matrix.
The proposed phase-structure mechanism would be disfavored if no B2 phase forms and the single-phase BCC alloy shows no ductility improvement.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and predicted outcome assert a marginal density increase, whereas the uncertainty field states that Al addition may instead reduce density. The stated rationale that low-mass Al causes a density increase is also internally questionable.

The baseline is already described as a single-phase continuous BCC matrix, but the mechanism describes B2 formation as converting a continuous brittle matrix into an inverted structure with a continuous BCC matrix. No actual matrix-phase inversion from the stated baseline is defined.

The target B2 morphology is described both as a discrete precipitate population and as a reticulated network. Those terms imply different connectivity, and the falsification rule does not establish a quantitative connectivity criterion separating the desired network from isolated particles or a continuous B2 matrix.
